strengths: The core idea of formulating robot morphology and reward co-design as a dialectical multi-agent LLM debate (thesis, antithesis, synthesis) with simulator feedback is intuitive and conceptually interesting.
The paper is clearly written and easy to follow, with well-structured diagrams (Figure 1 and Algorithm 1) illustrating the proposed workflow.
The qualitative observation that reward shaping co-evolves with morphological modifications highlights an important aspect of embodied design.
weaknesses: Extremely limited experimental evaluation: The proposed framework is evaluated on only a single task (Brax Ant locomotion) over merely five debate rounds. A robust co-design study requires testing across diverse morphologies (e.g., Walker2d, Humanoid, Quadruped/manipulator variants) and varied terrain/tasks.

Complete lack of comparative baselines: The method is only compared against the unoptimized default Ant baseline. There are no comparisons to established robot co-design methods (e.g., evolutionary algorithms, CMA-ES, bilevel RL), nor to recent LLM-based morphology or reward design baselines (such as Eureka, RoboMorph, or RoboMoRe), nor even standard random/heuristic search.

Absence of ablation studies: The paper does not provide empirical ablations to validate its key claims. Specifically, there is no evidence demonstrating that the multi-agent debate format outperforms a standard single-agent LLM pipeline, nor any ablation demonstrating the necessity or impact of the panel of pluralistic judges.

Premature manuscript scope and length: With only 4 pages of technical content, the submission resembles a preliminary workshop extended abstract rather than a comprehensive, fully developed ICML main track submission.

Missing technical and reproducibility details: The paper lacks essential implementation details, including the full prompt templates for the agents and judges, exact search spaces/constraints for morphology edits, PPO hyperparameter settings, and compute costs.

strengths: The conceptual formulation of framing robot co-design (morphology and reward shaping) as a dialectical debate (thesis, antithesis, synthesis) grounded in physical simulation is an intuitive and interesting idea.
The paper appropriately separates training rewards (tailored by the control agent) from an objective standardized evaluation metric to prevent reward hacking.
The pipeline and agent roles (design agent, control agent, pluralistic judges, hall-of-fame archive) are clearly illustrated in Figure 1 and Algorithm 1.
weaknesses: Severe internal inconsistency in reported experimental results: Figure 2 reports 'Distance from Origin' exceeding 50,000 for Round 5 (with a synthesis advantage of +36,171.5), whereas Table 1 and the main text report a top score of 6,421.67 and a 73% improvement over the default Ant score of 3,715.42. This discrepancy undermines the credibility of the empirical evaluation.

Extremely limited evaluation: The framework is tested on only a single task (Brax Ant) across just 5 debate rounds. A robust co-design study requires testing across diverse morphologies, environments, and obstacle/terrain conditions.

Lack of baselines and ablation studies: There are no comparisons to existing co-design literature (such as RoboMoRe, LASeR, or classic evolutionary/Bayesian co-design algorithms), nor any comparison to a single-agent baseline. Furthermore, the individual contributions of the dialectical debate, the pluralistic judges, and the synthesis step are not ablated.

Reproducibility and specification concerns: Section II-B states that 'both agents are instantiated with GPT-5', a model that is unreleased and not publicly available, making the experimental setup unverifiable and non-reproducible.

Submission format and maturity: The manuscript is structured as a 4-page extended abstract rather than a complete, rigorous conference submission, missing critical methodological details, prompt specifications, and in-depth qualitative/quantitative analysis.

strengths: Tackles the important and challenging problem of robot co-design (jointly optimizing morphology and reward/control), which is traditionally hindered by high-dimensional search spaces.
Grounding the multi-agent LLM debate in an actual physics simulator (Brax) provides objective, quantitative feedback to guide iterative LLM reasoning, avoiding pure hallucination.
The paper is clearly written, easy to follow, and the conceptual pipeline (thesis-antithesis-synthesis) is illustrated cleanly in Figure 1 and Algorithm 1.
weaknesses: Extremely narrow experimental scope: The evaluation is conducted on only a single simple environment (Brax Ant locomotion) over just 5 rounds, which is insufficient to validate the generality or robustness of the proposed framework.

Lack of essential baselines: The method is only compared against the default/unoptimized Ant baseline. There are no comparisons against relevant LLM-based co-design or design baselines (such as RoboMoRe, RoboMorph, or Eureka adapted to design), nor against standard non-LLM co-design methods (e.g., CMA-ES, Bayesian Optimization, or evolutionary algorithms).

Missing ablation studies: Key components of the system—such as the multi-agent debate structure vs. a single agent, the impact of the 'pluralistic judges' panel, and co-design vs. optimizing morphology or reward independently—are not ablated or isolated empirically.

Insufficient technical depth and completeness: At roughly 4 pages of main content, the paper resembles an extended abstract or workshop submission rather than a complete conference paper. Crucial details regarding exact prompt structures, parameter bounds, seed variability across full runs, and computational costs are missing.

strengths: Principled and well-motivated framework: The paper introduces a structured dialectical debate (thesis–antithesis–synthesis) specifically adapted for morphology–reward co-design, cleanly decoupling qualitative LLM reasoning/critique from objective physics-grounded evaluation and selection.

Comprehensive empirical validation: Evaluated across five standard locomotion benchmarks (Ant, HalfCheetah, Hopper, Swimmer, Walker2D) against competitive baselines including RoboMoRe, Eureka, and Bayesian Optimization, demonstrating substantial gains over baseline methods under compute-matched conditions.

In-depth ablations and analytical rigor: The authors methodically ablate the core architectural choices (iterative debate vs. zero-shot, role specialization vs. single-agent, synthesis step, and pluralistic judges) and provide multi-objective Pareto hypervolume analysis, AST-based reward syntax analysis, and critique-action correlation statistics.

Insightful cross-over analysis: Table 1 presents a clean difference-in-differences analysis isolating the individual contributions of morphology edits and reward shaping, convincingly demonstrating super-additive co-design synergy in 4 out of 5 tasks as well as reward transferability to unmodified default bodies.

Extensive transparency and reproducibility: The appendix provides exhaustive details including exact prompt templates, RL training hyperparameters, wall-clock/token cost breakdowns, and LLM backbone sensitivity tests.
weaknesses: Restricted morphology space and sim-to-real considerations: The morphological search space is confined to continuous parameter tuning within fixed kinematic topologies (MuJoCo XML templates) rather than discovering arbitrary new topologies or discrete joint assemblies, and the resulting aggressive gaits/morphologies may exploit simulator-specific dynamics without real-world manufacturability or torque constraints.

Small number of search seeds: The search phase relies on only 3 independent seeds per environment due to computational constraints, which is relatively small given the stochastic nature of both LLM generation and RL policy training (although the 5 re-evaluation seeds and Hedges' g effect sizes help mitigate this).

Uneven co-design benefit across environments: In simpler or low-DOF dynamics like Swimmer, gains are almost entirely dominated by morphology modification alone (resulting in a negative difference-in-differences interaction term), showing that dialectical reward co-design offers diminishing returns when task mechanics do not present complex control trade-offs.

strengths: Co-design of robot morphology and reward functions is a challenging problem characterized by tight non-linear coupling, and the idea of formulating this as a multi-agent debate (design agent vs. control agent with pluralistic judges) is conceptually intuitive.
Grounding LLM debate proposals in physics-based simulation (Brax) ensures that candidate selection and ranking are driven by empirical rollout performance rather than subjective LLM self-evaluation.

The experimental evaluation includes extensive ablations (evaluating iterative debate vs. zero-shot, role separation vs. single agent, thesis-antithesis synthesis vs. thesis-only, judge panel impact, and LLM backbone sensitivity).

The manuscript is clearly written and provides commendable documentation in the appendix, including full system/user prompts, RL hyperparameters, AST-based reward similarity analysis, compute costs, and example transcripts.
weaknesses: Evaluation metric disconnect and potential specification gaming: The standardized score $S = \sum_{t=0}^{T-1} d_t$ (cumulative distance from origin) heavily rewards unconstrained forward velocity and longer strides, but abstracts away balance costs and energy penalties present in standard benchmark rewards. Crucially, Table 10 reveals that the top-10 overlap between $S$ and standard episode returns is virtually nonexistent (0/10 for Swimmer and Walker2D, 1/10 for Ant and Hopper, averaging 1.0/10), indicating that the optimized candidates may be exploiting the custom surrogate metric rather than solving the canonical benchmark tasks.

Restricted morphology design space: Despite being framed as 'robot co-design', the morphology optimization is strictly limited to continuous parameter tuning (6 to 24 exposed scalar parameters like segment lengths and radii within a fixed kinematic XML template). It does not explore topological variation, limb addition, or discrete structural choices, which reduces the task to continuous hyperparameter optimization where classical evolutionary strategies (e.g., CMA-ES) are typically strong baselines.

Unconvincing baseline comparisons: Both Bayesian Optimization and RoboMoRe completely fail ($S = 0$) on Hopper and Walker2D across all seeds. Having two primary baselines collapse to zero on standard locomotion benchmarks suggests either inadequate hyperparameter tuning/priors or an excessively unforgiving search setup for continuous baselines, weakening the comparative claims.

Physical plausibility and sim-to-real transfer: The discovered morphologies shown in Figure 4 (e.g., extremely elongated and thin ant legs, highly asymmetric Walker2D limbs) appear to exploit simulation artifacts (e.g., simplified rigid body contact models in Brax) without accounting for actuator torque limits, structural deflection, or manufacturability constraints.

Small sample size for search: The search phase is run across only 3 random seeds per environment ($n=3$). Given the high stochasticity of both LLM generation and deep RL policy training, 3 seeds are insufficient to draw rigorous statistical conclusions, as reflected in the high variance in Table 7.

strengths: Innovative formulation of joint robot morphology and reward co-design as a structured dialectical multi-agent debate (thesis-antithesis-synthesis) coupled with role-specialized pluralistic LLM judges.

Rigorous grounding: unlike purely prompt-driven multi-agent LLM systems, candidate evaluation and selection are strictly governed by physics-based simulation in Brax, preventing hallucinatory selection loops.
Strong empirical gains over competitive baselines (including RoboMoRe, Eureka, and Bayesian Optimization) across five standard MuJoCo locomotion environments.

Comprehensive ablation and analysis suite examining key components: iterative debate vs. zero-shot compute-matched search, single-agent vs. role-separated debate, impact of pluralistic judges on Pareto coverage, reward transferability to default morphologies, and LLM backbone sensitivity.
High clarity and reproducibility with extensive appendix details, including full prompts, execution error handling, AST analysis of generated reward code, RL hyperparameters, and debate transcripts.
weaknesses: The search phase is evaluated over only n=3 search seeds per environment due to computational constraints, which limits statistical power, although final candidates are subsequently retrained over 5 seeds.
The design space is restricted to parametric scaling of predefined kinematic topologies rather than open-ended morphological or topological graph generation.

High RL computational budget: each run requires 80 full policy training runs per seed (~40 GPU hours per environment), which may limit immediate accessibility and scaling to more complex systems without surrogate modeling.

The primary evaluation metric is cumulative distance-from-origin rather than the canonical MuJoCo task reward; although Appendix H provides a thorough correlation analysis justifying this choice, standard forward velocity or canonical returns would provide additional validation.
